questions.q: Compute (4 − 3i)(4 + 3i).

weeks.prep: Tennis ball, phone that records video (slow-motion helps), a wall or doorframe with tape marks every foot (or meter), stopwatch. Desmos regression: type a table and y1 ~ ax1² + bx1 + c.
misconceptions: Thinking the parabola is the path in the air across the room. In the lab the graph is height vs TIME; a ball tossed straight up still produces a parabola in time.
Accepting a negative time or a negative length as an answer. Always state the domain that makes sense in context and reject nonviable solutions.

days.guide: Toss the ball straight up next to the taped wall while the phone records. Step through the video to record height every 0.1 s (or every few frames). Enter points in Desmos and fit y ~ ax² + bx + c.

questions.q: Why should the data be quadratic, and what should a be close to?
questions.a: Gravity gives constant downward acceleration, so height vs time is a parabola. In feet a ≈ −16 (half of −32 ft/s²); in meters a ≈ −4.9.

days.guide: Student uses the regression to find the vertex (max height) and positive zero (landing time) and compares the a-value to −16 (or −4.9). Today's task from the plan: Use the regression to find max height and landing time; compare to h = −16t² + v₀t + h₀. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: For h = −16t² + 48t + 6, find the maximum height and when it lands.
questions.a: Vertex at t = −48/(2·−16) = 1.5 s; h = −36 + 72 + 6 = 42 ft. Landing: −16t² + 48t + 6 = 0 → t = (48 + √2688)/32 ≈ 3.12 s (reject the negative root).

days.guide: Model solving y = x², y = x + 2 by substitution and showing the two crossing points in Desmos. Discuss 0, 1, or 2 intersections. Today's task from the plan: Solve algebraically and graphically (e.g., a line crossing a parabola). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve y = x² and y = x + 2.

days.guide: Model the fencing problem: 40 ft of fence, A = x(20 − x). Then revenue R = p(200 − 10p). Student finds each vertex and interprets. Today's task from the plan: Solve a fencing/area and a revenue (price × quantity) maximization problem. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What dimensions maximize the area with 40 ft of fence?
questions.a: A = x(20 − x) has vertex at x = 10: a 10 ft × 10 ft square, 100 sq ft.

questions.q: If quantity sold is 200 − 10p, what price maximizes revenue?
questions.a: R = 200p − 10p², vertex p = 10: price $10, revenue $1,000.

Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Solve x² − 6x + 13 = 0.

Unit 2 test sample answers: (x−1)²−9 → zeros −2, 4; 2x²+x−6=0 → 3/2, −2; x²+2x+3=0 → −1±i√2; (2−i)/(2+i) = (3−4i)/5; max of −5t²+20t+1 is 21 at t=2; y=2x+3 and y=x² meet at (3, 9) and (−1, 1).

weeks.prep: Algebra tiles or area-model templates. Have the student review exponent rules from Algebra I.
misconceptions: Writing (x + 2)² = x² + 4 (forgetting the middle term). Draw the area model: the two 2x rectangles are part of the square.
Subtracting only the first term of the second polynomial. Rewrite subtraction as adding the opposite and distribute the negative to every term.

days.guide: Model naming polynomials by degree and number of terms. Student classifies 10 polynomials and rewrites each in standard form. Today's task from the plan: Classify polynomials by degree and terms; write in standard form. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Classify 4x³ − 2x + 7 and write 5 − 3x² + x⁴ in standard form.
questions.a: 4x³ − 2x + 7: cubic trinomial (degree 3, three terms). 5 − 3x² + x⁴ = x⁴ − 3x² + 5, a quartic trinomial.

days.guide: Model combining like terms vertically. Discuss closure: integers + integers stay integers; polynomials ± and × stay polynomials. Today's task from the plan: Combine polynomials and discuss closure compared with integers. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Simplify (3x² − 2x + 5) − (x² + 4x − 1).
Are polynomials closed under division? Give an example.
questions.a: No. 1 ÷ x = 1/x (x⁻¹) is not a polynomial.

days.guide: Use an area grid to multiply (2x − 1)(x² + 3x − 4), then expand (x + 2)³ as (x + 2)(x + 2)². Today's task from the plan: Multiply polynomials with area models and distribution, including (x+2)³. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Expand (x + 2)³.
Multiply (2x − 1)(x² + 3x − 4).

days.guide: Prove an identity by expanding one side until it matches the other. Use (x² − y²)² + (2xy)² = (x² + y²)² to make Pythagorean triples. Today's task from the plan: Prove (a+b)² and a³−b³ identities; use x²+y² identity to generate Pythagorean triples. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Use x = 3, y = 2 in the identity to make a Pythagorean triple.
Verify a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²).
questions.a: (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) = a³ + a²b + ab² − a²b − ab² − b³ = a³ − b³.

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes) including one written proof. Today's task from the plan: Quiz on operations and a written proof of one identity. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Expand (x − 3)².

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) (4x³+x−2)+(x³−5x+9) = 5x³−4x+7. 2) (2x²−x)−(5x²+3x−4) = −3x²−4x+4. 3) (x−4)(x+4) = x²−16. 4) (3x+2)(x²−x+1) = 3x³−x²+x+2. 5) (2x−1)³ = 8x³−12x²+6x−1. Proof rubric (4 levels): 4 = expands one side completely, each step justified, ends with the other side; 3 = correct with a skipped step; 2 = partial expansion; 1 = substitutes numbers only (numbers check but do not prove).

weeks.prep: Practice set of division problems. Remind the student of numerical long division (divide, multiply, subtract, bring down).
misconceptions: Leaving out missing terms (e.g., dividing x³ − 7x + 6 without a 0x² placeholder). Always write every power with zeros as placeholders.
Using +3 instead of −3 in synthetic division for the divisor x + 3. The number in the box is the zero of the divisor: x + 3 = 0 → −3.

days.guide: Model (x³ + 2x² − 5x − 6) ÷ (x − 2) side by side with 1,452 ÷ 12. Student does five long divisions. Today's task from the plan: Divide polynomials by binomials using long division, connecting to numerical long division. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Divide (2x² + 5x − 1) ÷ (x + 3).
questions.a: 2x − 1 with remainder 2: (2x² + 5x − 1) = (x + 3)(2x − 1) + 2.

days.guide: Model synthetic division for the same problem as Day 1, comparing time. Student does eight synthetic divisions. Today's task from the plan: Use synthetic division for divisors of the form x−a; compare speed. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Divide (x³ − 7x + 6) ÷ (x + 3) synthetically.
questions.a: Use −3 with coefficients 1, 0, −7, 6: bottom row 1, −3, 2, 0 → x² − 3x + 2, remainder 0.

questions.q: Divide (x³ + 2x² − 5x − 6) ÷ (x − 2).
questions.a: Bottom row 1, 4, 3, 0 → x² + 4x + 3, remainder 0.

days.guide: Have the student compute p(3) directly and by synthetic division with 3; they match. State the Remainder Theorem. Today's task from the plan: Verify that p(a) equals the remainder; use it to evaluate p(3) quickly. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: For p(x) = x³ − 4x² + x + 5, find p(3) and the remainder of p(x) ÷ (x − 3).
questions.a: p(3) = 27 − 36 + 3 + 5 = −1, and the remainder is also −1.

days.guide: Remainder 0 means x − a is a factor. Model factoring x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 given root 1. Student factors four cubics. Today's task from the plan: Determine whether x−a is a factor and fully factor cubics given one root. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Factor x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 given that x = 1 is a zero.
questions.a: Synthetic with 1 gives x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3), so (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3).

questions.q: Is x + 1 a factor of x³ + 1?

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on division methods and theorems. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Find the remainder when x⁴ − 3x + 2 is divided by x − 2.

weeks.prep: Desmos for checking zeros. Make a reference card: a³ ± b³ = (a ± b)(a² ∓ ab + b²).
misconceptions: Factoring x³ − 27 as (x − 3)³. Expand (x − 3)³ to show it is different; use the difference-of-cubes pattern.
Listing only p/q with positive signs in the Rational Root Theorem. Every candidate needs ±.

days.guide: Model a³ − b³ and a³ + b³ (SOAP: Same, Opposite, Always Positive) and quadratic-form polynomials. Student factors eight. Today's task from the plan: Factor sums/differences of cubes and quadratic-form polynomials like x⁴−5x²+4. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Factor x³ − 27 and 8x³ + 1.
Factor x⁴ − 5x² + 4 completely.

days.guide: Model grouping the first two and last two terms and pulling out the common binomial. Student factors six. Today's task from the plan: Factor four-term polynomials by grouping. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Factor x³ + 3x² − 4x − 12.

days.guide: Model listing ±(factors of constant)/(factors of leading coefficient), testing with synthetic division, and factoring the quotient. Today's task from the plan: List possible rational roots and test with synthetic division. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Find the zeros of 2x³ − 3x² − 11x + 6.

days.guide: State the Fundamental Theorem: a degree-n polynomial has exactly n complex zeros counting multiplicity. Model finding complex zeros after factoring out real ones.

questions.q: Find all zeros of x³ − x² + 4x − 4.
Find all zeros of x⁴ − 16.

days.guide: Give the quiz: five polynomials, all zeros with multiplicities (about 35 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz: find all zeros of five polynomials and state multiplicities. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: State the zeros and multiplicities of f(x) = (x − 1)²(x + 3).
questions.a: x = 1 with multiplicity 2; x = −3 with multiplicity 1.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) x³−4x = x(x−2)(x+2): 0, 2, −2 (each mult. 1). 2) x³+2x²+x = x(x+1)²: 0 (1), −1 (2). 3) x³−2x²−9x+18 = (x−2)(x−3)(x+3): 2, 3, −3. 4) x⁴−13x²+36 = (x−2)(x+2)(x−3)(x+3): ±2, ±3. 5) x³+8 = (x+2)(x²−2x+4): −2, 1±i√3. Full credit requires all zeros (including complex) and multiplicities.

weeks.prep: Desmos and graph paper. Prepare a few printed polynomial graphs for Day 4 and the quiz.
misconceptions: Thinking a zero with multiplicity 2 crosses the axis. Even multiplicity touches and turns (bounces); odd crosses (multiplicity 3 flattens as it crosses).
Forgetting to use the y-intercept to find the leading coefficient when writing an equation from a graph.

days.guide: In Desmos, graph x², x³, −x⁴, −x⁵ and record end behavior in a 2×2 table (even/odd degree × positive/negative lead). Today's task from the plan: Investigate how degree and leading coefficient determine end behavior using Desmos. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Describe the end behavior of f(x) = −2x⁵ + 3x² − 1.
questions.a: Odd degree, negative leading coefficient: as x → ∞, f(x) → −∞; as x → −∞, f(x) → +∞.

days.guide: Graph y = (x − 1), (x − 1)², (x − 1)³ and compare behavior at x = 1. Today's task from the plan: Explore how even vs. odd multiplicity affects the graph at a zero. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How does y = (x + 2)²(x − 3) behave at each zero?
questions.a: At x = −2 (multiplicity 2) it touches and turns; at x = 3 (multiplicity 1) it crosses.

days.guide: Model the sketch checklist: degree & end behavior, zeros & multiplicity, y-intercept, then a smooth curve. Student sketches y = (x + 2)(x − 1)²(x − 4) and two more.

questions.q: List the features of y = (x + 2)(x − 1)²(x − 4).
questions.a: Degree 4, leading coefficient positive: both ends up. Crosses at −2 and 4, bounces at 1. y-intercept (2)(1)(−4) = −8.

days.guide: Give one polynomial as a graph and one as an equation; student compares zeros, end behavior, and approximate maximum. Today's task from the plan: Compare a polynomial given by graph to one given by equation (max, zeros, end behavior). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Which has more real zeros: f(x) = x³ − x, or a graph that crosses the x-axis only once?
questions.a: f(x) = x(x − 1)(x + 1) has three real zeros (−1, 0, 1), so f has more.

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 35 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz: sketch three polynomials and write equations from two graphs. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Write a cubic with zeros −3 (cross) and 2 (bounce) passing through (0, 12).

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: sketches graded on end behavior (1), zeros with correct cross/bounce (2), y-intercept (1). Sketch 1: y=x(x−3)² — starts low, crosses at 0, bounces at 3, ends high. Sketch 2: y=−(x+1)(x−2)(x−4) — up on left, down on right, crosses −1, 2, 4, y-int −8. Sketch 3: y=(x−1)³ — flattens and crosses at 1, y-int −1. Equations: graph with zeros −2, 1, 3 (all crossing) and y-int 6 → y=(x+2)(x−1)(x−3); quartic bouncing at ±2 with y-int 16 opening up → y=(x−2)²(x+2)².

weeks.prep: Cardstock (letter size 8.5 × 11 in), scissors, ruler, tape. Draw Pascal's triangle to row 6 yourself.
misconceptions: In the binomial expansion, forgetting to raise the coefficient (e.g., the 2 in 2x) to the power. Put each term in parentheses: (2x)³ = 8x³.
In the box problem, allowing x values that make a side negative. The domain is 0 < x < (shorter side)/2.

days.guide: Each corner square is x in; student builds boxes with x = 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5 in, measures volume, then models V(x) = x(11 − 2x)(8.5 − 2x) and finds the max in Desmos.

questions.q: What cut size maximizes volume for an 8.5 × 11 sheet, and what is the domain?
questions.a: Domain 0 < x < 4.25. Maximum at x ≈ 1.59 in, V ≈ 66.1 in³.

days.guide: Build Pascal's triangle (each entry = sum of two above). Expand (a + b)² and (a + b)³ and match coefficients. Today's task from the plan: Build Pascal's triangle and connect rows to (a+b)^n coefficients. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is row 4 of Pascal's triangle and what does it give?
questions.a: 1, 4, 6, 4, 1 — the coefficients of (a + b)⁴ = a⁴ + 4a³b + 6a²b² + 4ab³ + b⁴.

days.guide: Model (2x − 3)⁴ using C(4, k)(2x)^(4−k)(−3)^k. Then find one term of (x + 2)⁷ without expanding. Today's task from the plan: Expand (2x−3)⁴ and find a specific term using combinations. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Expand (2x − 3)⁴.
Find the x³ term of (x + 2)⁷.

days.guide: Model profit = revenue − cost with function notation. Student adds/multiplies two functions and interprets. Today's task from the plan: Add and multiply functions (e.g., revenue minus cost = profit) and interpret. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: R(x) = 15x and C(x) = 5x + 2000. Write P(x) and find the break-even point.
questions.a: P(x) = 10x − 2000; break-even when P = 0: x = 200 units.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test (about 50 minutes) and collect the box lab write-up. Today's task from the plan: Unit 3 test on polynomial operations, zeros, graphs, and modeling. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Find the remainder of x³ + 2x² − x + 4 divided by x + 1.

weeks.assessment_key: Box lab rubric: measured volumes table (1), correct V(x) and domain (1), max found (x≈1.59 in, V≈66.1 in³ for letter paper) (1), comparison of physical boxes to the model (1). Unit 3 test sample answers: (x²−3x+2)(x+4) = x³+x²−10x+8; zeros of x³−7x−6 = −1, −2, 3; (x+1)⁵ coefficients 1,5,10,10,5,1; end behavior of −x⁴: both down; x²+4x+5 zeros −2±i.

weeks.prep: Practice set. Remind the student how to simplify numerical fractions and find LCDs.
misconceptions: Cancelling terms instead of factors, e.g., (x + 3)/(x + 5) → 3/5. Only common FACTORS cancel; factor first.
Forgetting excluded values from the original denominator after a factor cancels.

days.guide: Model factoring numerator and denominator, cancelling common factors, and listing excluded values from the ORIGINAL denominator. Today's task from the plan: Factor and simplify rational expressions, stating excluded values. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Simplify (x² − 9)/(x² + 5x + 6) and state excluded values.

days.guide: Model multiply = factor everything then cancel; divide = multiply by the reciprocal. Today's task from the plan: Multiply and divide rational expressions with factoring. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Simplify (x/3) ÷ (x²/6).

days.guide: Model finding the LCD from factored denominators and rewriting each fraction. Today's task from the plan: Find LCDs and add/subtract rational expressions. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Simplify 3/x + 2/(x + 1).
Simplify 1/(x − 2) − 4/(x² − 4).

days.guide: Method 1: simplify top and bottom then divide. Method 2: multiply top and bottom by the LCD of all small fractions. Compare. Today's task from the plan: Simplify complex fractions by two methods and compare. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Simplify (1 + 1/x)/(1 − 1/x²).
questions.a: Multiply by x²: (x² + x)/(x² − 1) = x(x + 1)/((x − 1)(x + 1)) = x/(x − 1).

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on rational expression operations. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Simplify (2x + 6)/(x² − 9).

weeks.prep: Desmos. Look up Boyle's law (pressure × volume constant at fixed temperature).
misconceptions: Thinking a graph can never cross a horizontal asymptote. Horizontal asymptotes describe end behavior only; graph y = x/(x² + 1) to see it cross y = 0.
Calling every zero of the denominator a vertical asymptote. If the factor cancels, it is a hole.

days.guide: Introduce y = k/x. Model finding k from one data point. Graph and discuss why y never reaches 0. Today's task from the plan: Model Boyle's law-type inverse variation and graph y = k/x. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: y varies inversely with x and y = 6 when x = 4. Find y when x = 8.
A gas at 2 atm occupies 6 L. At constant temperature, what is its volume at 3 atm?
questions.a: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂: 12 = 3V, V = 4 L.

days.guide: Treat y = a/(x − h) + k like any transformation: asymptotes x = h and y = k. Today's task from the plan: Graph y = a/(x−h)+k and identify asymptotes. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Give the asymptotes of y = 3/(x + 2) − 1.
questions.a: Vertical x = −2; horizontal y = −1.

days.guide: Model factoring, finding holes (cancelled factors), vertical asymptotes (remaining denominator zeros), and horizontal asymptote by comparing degrees. Today's task from the plan: Find vertical asymptotes, holes, and horizontal asymptotes from factored forms. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Find holes and asymptotes of f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x² − x − 2).
questions.a: (x − 1)(x + 1)/((x − 2)(x + 1)): hole at x = −1 (point (−1, 2/3)), vertical asymptote x = 2, horizontal asymptote y = 1.

days.guide: Model dividing (2x + 3) by (x − 1) to get 2 + 5/(x − 1), and read the graph as 5/x shifted right 1, up 2. Today's task from the plan: Use long division to rewrite (2x+3)/(x−1) as 2 + 5/(x−1) and interpret the graph. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Rewrite (2x + 3)/(x − 1) and name its asymptotes.
questions.a: 2 + 5/(x − 1) (since 2(x − 1) + 5 = 2x + 3). Vertical x = 1, horizontal y = 2.

days.guide: Give the quiz: graph three rational functions with all features labeled (about 35 minutes). Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What is the horizontal asymptote of y = 3x/(x² + 4)?
questions.a: Degree of denominator is greater, so y = 0.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) y=1/(x−3)+2: VA x=3, HA y=2, y-int 5/3, x-int 5/2. 2) y=(x+1)/(x−2): VA x=2, HA y=1, x-int −1, y-int −1/2. 3) y=(x²−4)/(x−2): hole at (2, 4), otherwise the line y = x+2, no asymptotes. Each graph: 1 pt each for VA, HA/hole, intercepts, correct branches.

weeks.prep: Practice set. Prepare one 'two pipes' and one boat-current problem. Calculator allowed.
misconceptions: Not checking solutions in the original equation. Any value that makes an original denominator zero is extraneous.
Averaging speeds (e.g., 60 and 40 → 50) for a round trip. Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.

days.guide: Model multiplying both sides by the LCD, solving, then checking each answer against excluded values. Today's task from the plan: Solve rational equations by multiplying by the LCD; check for extraneous solutions. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve 3/x + 1/2 = 2.
questions.a: Multiply by 2x: 6 + x = 4x, x = 2. Check: 1.5 + 0.5 = 2 ✓.
x = 3 + 2(x − 3) → x = 3, which makes a denominator zero: extraneous, so no solution.

days.guide: Model 'work rate = 1/time' and adding rates. Student solves four job problems. Today's task from the plan: Solve 'two pipes fill a tank' and shared-job problems. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Pipe A fills a tank in 6 h, pipe B in 3 h. Together?
questions.a: 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 tank per hour, so 2 hours.

days.guide: Model a d = rt table for upstream and downstream. Student solves three rate problems. Today's task from the plan: Solve upstream/downstream and average-speed problems. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: A boat goes 12 mph in still water against a 3 mph current for 30 miles, then back. Total time?
questions.a: Upstream 30/9 = 3⅓ h, downstream 30/15 = 2 h; total 5⅓ h (5 h 20 min).

questions.q: Find the periods of y = sin(4x) and y = cos(x/2).

questions.a: π/6 to the right.

weeks.prep: Desmos in radian mode.
misconceptions: Thinking tan x has a maximum of 1 like sine. Tangent's range is all real numbers.
Placing secant asymptotes where cosine is 1. Secant is undefined where cosine is 0.

days.guide: Build tan x = sin x/cos x: zeros where sin = 0, asymptotes where cos = 0. Today's task from the plan: Graph y = tan x from sin/cos ratios and identify asymptotes and period π. questions.q: Give the period, zeros, and asymptotes of y = tan x.
questions.a: Period π; zeros at x = kπ; vertical asymptotes at x = π/2 + kπ.

days.guide: Graph sin x, then csc x = 1/sin x on top: U-shapes touching the sine peaks. Today's task from the plan: Graph csc and sec from their reciprocal sine and cosine graphs. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Where are the asymptotes of y = csc x and what is its range?
questions.a: At x = kπ (where sin x = 0). Range y ≤ −1 or y ≥ 1.

days.guide: Graph cot x = cos x/sin x and compare with tan x. Today's task from the plan: Graph cot x and compare with tan x. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How does cot x differ from tan x?
questions.a: Asymptotes at x = kπ (instead of π/2 + kπ), zeros at π/2 + kπ, and it decreases on each interval while tan increases. Same period π.

days.guide: Apply a, b, h, k to tangent and secant in Desmos. Today's task from the plan: Apply transformations to tangent and secant graphs. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Find the period and asymptotes of y = 2 tan(x/2).
questions.a: Period π/(1/2) = 2π; asymptotes at x = π + 2kπ.

days.guide: Quiz: match six graphs to equations (about 25 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz matching six trig function graphs and equations. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Which graph has U-shaped pieces opening up at x = 0 and asymptotes at ±π/2?
questions.a: y = sec x.

Assuming the model is exact. Discuss residuals and why weather or geography make real data deviate.

questions.a: h(t) = −25cos(πt/5) + 30: amplitude 25, midline 30, period 10, starting at the minimum (5 m). At t = 5, h = 55 m (top).

days.guide: Enter monthly daylight hours and fit y = a cos(b(x − h)) + d by reading max, min, and period, then refine with Desmos regression. questions.q: If maximum daylight is 14.4 h (June) and minimum 9.9 h (December), find amplitude, midline, and period.
questions.a: Amplitude (14.4 − 9.9)/2 = 2.25 h; midline 12.15 h; period 12 months.

days.guide: Plot a day or two of NOAA hourly heights and fit a sinusoid. Today's task from the plan: Use NOAA tide data for a California station to model water height. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: High tide is 5.5 ft, low tide 0.5 ft. Give amplitude, midline, and an approximate period.
questions.a: Amplitude 2.5 ft, midline 3 ft, period about 12.4 hours (two highs per day).

days.guide: Student predicts a value from each model and compares to actual data, then writes two limitations. Today's task from the plan: Use models to predict values and compare to actual data; discuss model limits. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Name one limitation of a sinusoidal tide model.
questions.a: Real tides have unequal highs/lows (mixed tides), lunar-cycle changes, and weather effects, so a single sine with a fixed amplitude will drift from the data.

questions.q: Convert 225° to radians and evaluate its cosine.

Unit 7 sample answers: 240° = 4π/3; arc s for r=6, θ=π/3 is 2π; sin(3π/4)=√2/2; given cos θ=4/5 in QIV, sin θ=−3/5; period of y=4 sin(πx/6) is 12; y=tan x asymptotes at π/2+kπ.

Confusing arithmetic (add d) with geometric (multiply by r). Check differences and ratios first.

days.guide: Measure the height of 1, 2, 3, 4 nested cups. Write a recursive rule and an explicit rule. Today's task from the plan: Build a stacking-cup pattern and write recursive and explicit rules. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: A cup stack is 12 cm for 1 cup and grows 1.5 cm per added cup. Give recursive and explicit rules.
questions.a: Recursive: h₁ = 12, hₙ = hₙ₋₁ + 1.5. Explicit: hₙ = 12 + 1.5(n − 1).

days.guide: Model finding d, writing a_n, and finding any term. Today's task from the plan: Find terms and write formulas a_n = a₁ + (n−1)d. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: a₁ = 7, d = 4. Find a₂₀.
Write a formula for 3, 10, 17, ….

questions.q: Find a formula and the 8th term of 2, 6, 18, ….

Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: A ball dropped from 2 m rebounds to 60% of its height each time. How high after the 3rd bounce?

questions.q: Is 5, 10, 20, 40 arithmetic or geometric? Give the next term.
questions.a: Geometric with r = 2; next term 80.

Applying the infinite-series formula when |r| ≥ 1. Such series diverge (no finite sum).

Derive S − rS to get S_n = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r). Apply to a loan: payment = P·i/(1 − (1 + i)^(−n)). Today's task from the plan: Derive S_n = a(1−r^n)/(1−r) and apply to mortgage/loan payment problems. weeks.prep: Two or three recent news articles that report on a study (health or education topics work well). A random number generator (random.org or a calculator).
misconceptions: Concluding cause and effect from an observational study. Only a randomized experiment can support causation; observational studies show association.
Thinking a larger sample fixes bias. A huge convenience sample is still biased; how you sample matters more than how many.

days.guide: Define survey, experiment (treatment imposed), observational study (no treatment imposed). Student classifies 12 descriptions. Today's task from the plan: Classify 12 study descriptions as surveys, experiments, or observational studies. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Researchers compare heart health of people who already drink coffee with those who don't. Which type?
questions.a: Observational study: no treatment was assigned.

questions.q: Students are randomly assigned to study with or without music. Which type?
questions.a: Experiment: researchers impose the treatment with random assignment.

days.guide: Model each sampling method with a school-of-1,000 example. Identify bias types (undercoverage, nonresponse, voluntary response, wording). Today's task from the plan: Compare simple random, stratified, cluster, and convenience samples; identify bias. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How is stratified sampling different from cluster sampling?
questions.a: Stratified: divide into groups and randomly sample from EVERY group. Cluster: divide into groups, randomly pick some whole groups, and survey everyone in them.

questions.q: An online poll on a sports site asks readers to vote. Main bias?
questions.a: Voluntary response bias: people with strong opinions choose to respond.

days.guide: Student writes a design: question, treatments, random assignment method, control, replication, and what to measure. Today's task from the plan: Design a randomized experiment testing whether music affects reaction time. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Why randomize in the music/reaction-time experiment?
questions.a: To balance unknown variables (sleep, skill) between groups so differences can be attributed to music.

days.guide: Student reads two articles and writes an evaluation: study type, sample, possible bias, and whether the headline's claim is justified. Today's task from the plan: Critique two news articles reporting on data; write an evaluation. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: A headline says 'Eating breakfast causes better grades' based on a survey. Is this justified?
questions.a: No. A survey is observational; confounding variables (family routines, income, sleep) could explain the association.

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on study design and bias. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What is a confounding variable?
questions.a: A variable related to both the explanatory and response variables that makes it impossible to separate their effects.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) classify 5 scenarios (survey/experiment/observational). 2) name sampling method in 4 scenarios (SRS, stratified, cluster, convenience). 3) identify bias in a mall survey: undercoverage/convenience. 4) design rubric: random assignment (1), control/comparison group (1), replication (1), clear response variable (1). 5) Explain why causation cannot be concluded from an observational study.

weeks.prep: A data set of about 100 values (measure hand spans of family/friends or use published heights). Desmos normal distribution tool or a calculator with normalcdf.
misconceptions: Applying the 68-95-99.7 rule to skewed data. Check the histogram shape first.
Comparing raw scores across different tests. Convert to z-scores to compare relative standing.

days.guide: Make a histogram of the data set; describe shape, center, spread, and outliers. Today's task from the plan: Make histograms of a real data set (e.g., 100 measured hand spans) and describe shape. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: What does 'approximately normal' look like?
questions.a: Single-peaked, symmetric, bell-shaped, with mean ≈ median and few extreme values.

days.guide: Draw a normal curve with mean and ±1, 2, 3 SD marked; shade regions. Today's task from the plan: Apply the 68-95-99.7 rule to estimate percentages. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: IQ scores: mean 100, SD 15. What percent lie between 85 and 115? Above 130?
questions.a: About 68% (±1 SD). Above 130 is beyond +2 SD: about 2.5%.

days.guide: Model z = (x − μ)/σ. Compare two test results. Today's task from the plan: Calculate and compare z-scores (e.g., comparing ACT and SAT performance). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: SAT 1300 (mean 1050, SD 200) vs ACT 28 (mean 21, SD 5). Which is better relative to peers?
questions.a: SAT z = 1.25; ACT z = 1.4. The ACT score is relatively better.

days.guide: Use technology to find areas; discuss when the normal model is inappropriate (skewed incomes, wait times). Today's task from the plan: Use technology to find areas under the normal curve; recognize when a normal model is not appropriate. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: With mean 100 and SD 10, find P(X > 120).
Find P(Z < 1).

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on normal distributions. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: A z-score of −1.5 means what?
questions.a: The value is 1.5 standard deviations below the mean.

weeks.prep: Coins, dice, and a spreadsheet with =RAND() or =RANDBETWEEN(). Find a current poll with a margin of error.
misconceptions: Interpreting a margin of error as covering all possible errors. It accounts only for random sampling variability, not biased questions or samples.
Thinking a single unusual result proves unfairness. Compare the result with the spread of many simulated results.

days.guide: Flip a coin 50 times and count heads. In a spreadsheet, simulate 100 sets of 50 fair flips and make a dot plot of head counts. Today's task from the plan: Flip a coin 50 times; simulate 100 sets in a spreadsheet to judge whether results are consistent with fairness. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: If you got 32 heads in 50 flips, is the coin likely unfair?
questions.a: With a fair coin, 32 or more heads happens only about 3% of the time, so 32 is unusual and gives some evidence the coin is unfair (but is not proof).

days.guide: Simulate 200 samples of size 50 from a population with p = 0.40; plot the sample proportions. Today's task from the plan: Simulate many samples of size 50 from a known population proportion and plot proportions. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Describe the distribution of sample proportions.
questions.a: Centered near 0.40, roughly bell-shaped, with most proportions within about ±0.14 (2 SD, since SD = √(0.4·0.6/50) ≈ 0.069).

days.guide: Estimate the margin of error as about 2 SD from the simulation and compare with 1/√n. Today's task from the plan: Estimate margin of error from simulation and compare to 1/√n. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: What is the approximate margin of error for n = 400? For n = 1,000?

questions.q: How would you use a die to choose fairly among three people?
questions.a: Assign 1–2, 3–4, 5–6 to each person; each has probability 1/3.

days.guide: Give the quiz on interpreting margins of error (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz interpreting a poll's margin of error. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: A poll says 52% support a measure, ±3%. Can you conclude a majority supports it?
questions.a: No. The plausible range is 49%–55%, which includes values below 50%.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) 45% ±4% → plausible 41%–49%. 2) Quadrupling n halves the margin of error. 3) n = 2,500 → MOE ≈ 2%. 4) Explain why a self-selected online poll's margin of error is meaningless (bias). 5) Simulation shows 18–32 heads covers about 95% of fair 50-flip results; decide whether 35 heads is unusual (yes).

weeks.prep: Index cards for shuffling data. Materials for the chosen experiment (paper for airplanes, measuring tape) — let the student choose by Day 2.
misconceptions: Concluding 'no effect' when a difference isn't significant. It means the data don't give convincing evidence, not proof of no difference.
Running all trials of one treatment first (e.g., when tired). Randomize the order of trials.

days.guide: Write each result from a two-group experiment on a card; shuffle into two piles many times and record the difference in means. Compare to the actual difference.

questions.q: If only 2 of 100 shuffles give a difference as large as observed, what do you conclude?
questions.a: About 2% chance by random assignment alone, so the difference is statistically significant (unlikely to be due to chance).

days.guide: Student writes question, two treatments, response variable, randomization plan, and controlled variables. Today's task from the plan: Design a randomized experiment with two treatments (e.g., paper airplane wing design) and collect data. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Name three variables to hold constant in a paper-airplane experiment.
questions.a: Paper type and size, launcher and launch force/angle, and location (indoors, no wind).

days.guide: Run at least 20 trials per treatment in random order; record carefully. Today's task from the plan: Run the experiment with at least 20 trials per treatment. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Why at least 20 trials per treatment?
questions.a: Replication reduces the effect of chance variation so a real difference is easier to detect.

days.guide: Compute means, medians, and SDs; run a randomization test (spreadsheet or by hand with many shuffles). Today's task from the plan: Analyze results with a randomization test and summary statistics. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What does the p-value from the randomization test mean in your project?
questions.a: The proportion of random re-shuffles giving a difference at least as large as observed: the chance of seeing this difference if the treatment had no effect.

days.guide: Collect the report and give the Unit 9 test (about 45 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Submit a statistics project report and take the Unit 9 test. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Why can a well-designed randomized experiment show causation?
questions.a: Random assignment balances other variables, so a significant difference can be attributed to the treatment.

weeks.assessment_key: Project rubric (4 levels): design (randomization, control, replication), data quality (≥20 per treatment), analysis (summary stats + randomization test), conclusion (answers question, states uncertainty and limitations). Proficient = clear design, correct statistics, and a conclusion that does not overclaim. Unit 9 test sample answers: experiment vs observational identification; z = (85−75)/5 = 2; 95% within 2 SD; MOE ≈ 1/√n; interpretation of a p-value of 0.30 → not significant.

weeks.prep: Help the student find a public data set: California Department of Finance population, NOAA monthly temperatures, etc. Desmos.
misconceptions: Choosing the model with the best R² even if it makes absurd predictions. A model must also make sense in context (e.g., population can't go negative).
Extrapolating far outside the data range. Discuss how uncertainty grows beyond the data.

days.guide: Student picks a data set of 15+ points and graphs it in Desmos, writing what pattern they see. Today's task from the plan: Choose a real data set and graph it. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: What pattern would you expect in 12 months of average temperatures?
questions.a: Periodic (sinusoidal), period 12 months.

days.guide: Fit linear, quadratic, exponential, and sinusoidal regressions; plot residuals for each. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does a good residual plot look like?
questions.a: Residuals scattered randomly around 0 with no curve or pattern.

days.guide: Student writes a one-page justification: chosen model, evidence (residuals, context), and limitations. Today's task from the plan: Write a justification for the best model, including limitations. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why might an exponential model fail for long-term population predictions?
questions.a: Resources limit growth; real populations level off (logistic), so exponential overpredicts.

days.guide: Student prepares a 5-minute presentation with a graph, model equation, predictions, and limits. Rehearse once. Today's task from the plan: Prepare a 5-minute presentation of the model and predictions. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What should every prediction slide include?
questions.a: The input value, predicted output with units, and a statement of confidence/limitations.

days.guide: Student presents; you ask two questions about model choice and limits. Today's task from the plan: Present the capstone and answer questions. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Your model predicts a value 30 years ahead. How confident should we be?
questions.a: Not very: extrapolation far beyond the data assumes the pattern continues, which is uncertain.

weeks.assessment_key: Capstone rubric (4 levels per row): Data (relevant, cited source, 15+ points); Models (at least 3 fitted, equations stated); Justification (residuals and context used to choose, limitations stated); Predictions (reasonable, within or near data range, with units); Presentation (clear, 5 minutes, answers questions). Proficient (3) = all rows present and correct with minor gaps.

weeks.prep: Final review packet (Khan Academy course challenge works well). Two quiet 60-minute exam blocks.
misconceptions: Spending review time only on favorite topics. Use the semester exam and quiz errors to target weak units.
Skipping the reflection. Error analysis is where most learning from an exam happens.

days.guide: Mixed review on Units 1–5; student marks unsure items to revisit. Today's task from the plan: Mixed review on quadratics, polynomials, rationals, and radicals. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve √(x + 5) = x − 1.

days.guide: Mixed review on Units 6–9. Today's task from the plan: Mixed review on exponentials, logs, trig, sequences, and statistics. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve 5e^(2t) = 40.
Find the sum of the infinite series 9 + 3 + 1 + ….

days.guide: Final part 1: non-calculator (60 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Non-calculator section. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Evaluate log₃81 + sin(π/6).

days.guide: Final part 2: calculator and modeling (60 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Calculator section with modeling tasks. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: $3,000 at 5% compounded monthly; when does it reach $5,000?

days.guide: Return the graded exam; student writes a reflection on each missed item and on readiness for Precalculus. Today's task from the plan: Review exam errors and write a reflection on growth and readiness for Precalculus. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What should an error reflection include?
questions.a: The item, what went wrong (concept vs careless), the correct solution, and one action to prevent it.

weeks.assessment_key: Final exam representative answers: (x−3)²+2 vertex (3,2); 2x²+7x+3 = (2x+1)(x+3); x³−6x²+11x−6 zeros 1, 2, 3; (x+1)/(x²−1) = 1/(x−1); 16^(3/4)=8; log₂(x)=5 → 32; cos(5π/3)=1/2; period of 3 sin(2x) is π; a₁₀ of 2, 6, 18 is 39,366; 95% of normal data within 2 SD. Grade bands: 90%+ excellent, 75–89% proficient, 60–74% basic (review before Precalculus), below 60% needs targeted summer work. Reflection rubric: complete error analysis for every missed item = full credit.

SCI.overview: Physics of the Universe is taught through phenomena and kitchen-table labs: most days have the student make a prediction, collect data (often with a phone video or a PhET simulation), and explain results in claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) form. Model one worked problem with units every time, then let the student do the rest; always ask 'what evidence supports that?'. Use g = 9.8 m/s² throughout, insist on units and significant figures, and review safety before each lab (eye protection for projectiles, never look at the Sun, adult supervision with heat and lasers).

weeks.prep: Toy car, meter stick, masking tape, phone with slow-motion video. Queue up a short crash-test video (IIHS has many). Make a large 'driving question board' on poster paper.
misconceptions: Confusing velocity and acceleration: a fast car is not necessarily accelerating. Acceleration is the rate of CHANGE of velocity; a car at a steady 30 m/s has zero acceleration.
Reading a position-time graph as a picture of the path. The slope is velocity; a flat line means the object is stopped, not moving along flat ground.

days.guide: Show the crash-test video twice. The student writes at least 10 questions about forces and safety and sorts them on the driving question board (we'll return to it in the egg-crash challenge).

questions.q: Why do crash-test dummies move forward when the car stops suddenly?
questions.a: They tend to keep moving at the car's original speed (inertia) until a force—seatbelt, airbag, or dashboard—stops them.

days.guide: Tape marks every meter for 5 m. Release the car and record the time at each mark (several trials). The student graphs position vs. time and finds the slope.

questions.q: A car's position-time graph is a straight line from (0 s, 0 m) to (4 s, 2 m). What is its velocity?
questions.a: Slope = 2 m ÷ 4 s = 0.5 m/s, constant velocity.

questions.q: What does a curved, steepening position-time graph mean?
questions.a: The object is speeding up (accelerating): the slope (velocity) increases.

days.guide: Film a ball rolling down a ramp in slow motion beside a meter stick. Step through frames to get position at equal time intervals, then compute velocities and acceleration a = Δv/Δt.

questions.q: A ball's velocity goes from 0.2 m/s to 1.0 m/s in 0.8 s. What is its acceleration?

days.guide: Model one braking problem using v² = v₀² + 2aΔx, writing knowns and unknowns first. The student solves five more. Today's task from the plan: Solve constant-acceleration problems (braking distances) using the kinematic equations. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: A car traveling 25 m/s brakes at −5.0 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping?
How long does that stop take?

days.guide: Give the quiz (30 minutes). Afterwards check graphs by acting them out (walk toward/away from a wall). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on motion graphs and kinematic calculations. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: A car accelerates from rest at 3 m/s² for 4 s. Find its final speed and distance.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key (sample): 1) slope of position-time = velocity. 2) horizontal line = at rest. 3) velocity-time slope = acceleration; area = displacement. 4) 0→20 m/s in 4 s: a = 5 m/s². 5) from rest at 2 m/s² for 5 s: v = 10 m/s, Δx = 25 m. 6) braking from 30 m/s at −6 m/s²: Δx = 75 m. 7) sketch: constant velocity = straight sloped line on x-t, flat line on v-t. 8) a ball thrown up has a = −9.8 m/s² even at the top. Score 1 pt each with units.

weeks.prep: Toy car, rubber bands, washers, a coin, an index card, a cup; a smooth plastic tablecloth and unbreakable dishes for the tablecloth trick. Open PhET 'Forces and Motion: Basics.'
misconceptions: Thinking a moving object needs a net force to keep moving. Newton's first law: with no net force it keeps moving at constant velocity; friction is what usually slows things down.
Labeling 'the force of motion' on free-body diagrams. Only real forces with an agent (gravity, normal, friction, tension, applied) appear.

days.guide: Do the coin-card-cup demo (flick the card; the coin drops into the cup) and the tablecloth pull. The student explains each with Newton's first law. Today's task from the plan: Perform coin-card-cup and tablecloth inertia demos; explain using Newton's first law. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why does the coin fall into the cup instead of flying off with the card?
questions.a: The flick acts on the card for a very short time with little friction on the coin; the coin's inertia keeps it nearly at rest, then gravity pulls it into the cup.

days.guide: Model a free-body diagram for a book on a table (weight down, normal up, equal). The student draws eight, including a car braking. Today's task from the plan: Draw free-body diagrams for 8 scenarios including a car braking and a book on a table. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Draw the forces on a car braking on a level road.
questions.a: Weight down, normal force up (equal), and friction from the road pointing backward (opposite motion); net force is backward, so it decelerates.

days.guide: Pull the car with a rubber band stretched the same length each time (constant force) while adding washers. Film and measure acceleration; graph a vs. mass.

questions.q: If the force stays the same and mass doubles, what happens to acceleration?
questions.a: It halves (a = F/m): an inverse relationship.

days.guide: In PhET, hold mass constant and vary applied force; record acceleration and graph a vs. F_net. Today's task from the plan: Use PhET Forces and Motion to test acceleration vs. net force; analyze the linear relationship. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: A 2.0 kg cart has a net force of 10 N. What is its acceleration?
What does the slope of the a vs. F graph represent?
questions.a: 1/m (the inverse of the mass).

days.guide: The student writes a CER explaining the lab data with Newton's second law. Today's task from the plan: Write a CER explaining your lab data using Newton's second law. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: State Newton's second law in words.
questions.a: An object's acceleration equals the net force on it divided by its mass, in the direction of the net force.

weeks.assessment_key: CER rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning). Claim: answers the question about how mass affects acceleration with a constant force in one sentence. Evidence: specific data from the student's own lab/simulation with numbers and units. Reasoning: connects the evidence to the scientific principle. A proficient response: 'Adding mass decreased the cart's acceleration' with data such as 'with 0 washers a ≈ 0.60 m/s², with 4 washers a ≈ 0.30 m/s²', and reasoning that with constant force a = F/m, so acceleration is inversely proportional to mass (graph curves downward, a vs 1/m is linear).

weeks.prep: Balloon, straw, 5 m of string, tape; a luggage scale (or spring scale reading in newtons; if it reads in kg, multiply by 9.8 to get N); a shoe; surfaces (tile, carpet, wood).
misconceptions: Believing action-reaction forces cancel. They act on DIFFERENT objects, so they can't cancel; only forces on the same object add up.
Thinking the normal force always equals weight. It changes on inclines (mg cos θ) and in accelerating elevators.

days.guide: Thread the string through the straw, tape on the inflated balloon, and release. The student identifies the force pair (balloon pushes air backward; air pushes balloon forward).

questions.q: When you push against a wall, what is the reaction force?
questions.a: The wall pushes back on you with an equal and opposite force.

days.guide: Drag the shoe at constant speed with the luggage scale on each surface. μ = friction force ÷ normal force (the shoe's weight in N). Today's task from the plan: Drag a shoe across different surfaces with a luggage scale; calculate coefficient of friction. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: A 1.0 kg shoe (weight 9.8 N) needs 3.0 N to drag at constant speed. What is μ?
Why drag at constant speed?
questions.a: Then net force is zero, so the scale reading equals the friction force.

days.guide: Model an incline (components) and an elevator problem. Today's task from the plan: Solve problems on inclines and elevators. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: A 60 kg person is in an elevator accelerating upward at 2.0 m/s². What does a scale read?
questions.a: N = m(g + a) = 60(11.8) = 708 N (they feel heavier).

questions.q: A 10 kg box sits on a 30° incline. What is the normal force?

days.guide: Discuss tire tread, anti-lock brakes, and wet roads; compute how stopping distance changes when μ falls. Today's task from the plan: Analyze how tires and brakes use friction; discuss stopping distance in rain. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why are stopping distances longer in rain?
questions.a: Water lowers the coefficient of friction between tires and road, so the maximum braking force (μN) is smaller, giving less deceleration and a longer stopping distance.

days.guide: Give the Newton's laws quiz (30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on Newton's laws problems. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: A 1,200 kg car accelerates at 2.5 m/s². What net force acts on it?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key (sample): 1) First law: objects keep their state of motion without net force. 2) 5 kg, 20 N net → 4 m/s². 3) Force pair example: foot pushes ground backward, ground pushes foot forward. 4) μ from 12 N friction on a 40 N box = 0.30. 5) 50 kg person in elevator accelerating down at 2 m/s² → N = 50(7.8) = 390 N. 6) Free-body diagram of hanging lamp: tension up = weight down. 7) Why action-reaction pairs don't cancel (different objects).

weeks.prep: Two toy cars of known mass (weigh on a kitchen scale), modeling clay, ruler, marbles; PhET Collision Lab. Eggs in zip-top bags, a towel, pillow, and hard floor protected with newspaper.
misconceptions: Thinking momentum is 'lost' in an inelastic collision. Total momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is what is partly converted to heat and sound.
Forgetting momentum is a vector. Objects moving in opposite directions have opposite signs.

days.guide: Model p = mv with units kg·m/s. The student calculates momentum for a truck, a baseball, a person walking. Today's task from the plan: Calculate momentum for everyday objects; compare a truck and a baseball. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Compare a 2,000 kg truck at 10 m/s to a 0.145 kg baseball at 40 m/s.
questions.a: Truck: 20,000 kg·m/s. Baseball: 5.8 kg·m/s. The truck has about 3,400 times more momentum.

days.guide: Film one car hitting a stationary car (with clay to make them stick). Measure speeds before and after and compare total momentum. Today's task from the plan: Collide toy cars (with clay for inelastic) and measure velocities from video to test momentum conservation. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: A 2.0 kg cart at 3.0 m/s sticks to a 1.0 kg cart at rest. Find their speed after.
questions.a: Total p = 6.0 kg·m/s = 3.0 kg × v → v = 2.0 m/s.

days.guide: In PhET, run elastic and inelastic collisions; record total momentum and kinetic energy before and after. Today's task from the plan: Use PhET Collision Lab to verify momentum conservation in elastic and inelastic collisions. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: In a perfectly elastic collision, what is conserved?
questions.a: Both total momentum and total kinetic energy.

days.guide: Drop a bagged egg from 1 m onto floor, towel, and pillow. Discuss impulse J = FΔt = Δp. Today's task from the plan: Drop an egg onto different surfaces (in a bag) and relate impulse = FΔt. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why does the egg survive on the pillow?
questions.a: The egg's change in momentum is the same, but the pillow increases the stopping time, so the average force (Δp/Δt) is much smaller.

questions.q: An egg (0.060 kg) hits at 4.4 m/s and stops in 0.010 s. Average force?
questions.a: Δp = 0.060 × 4.4 ≈ 0.26 kg·m/s; F = 0.26/0.010 ≈ 26 N (stopping in 0.10 s gives only 2.6 N).

days.guide: Give the momentum quiz (30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Solve conservation of momentum problems in a quiz. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: A 60 kg skater at rest pushes a 40 kg skater who moves off at 3 m/s. Velocity of the first skater?
questions.a: 0 = 40(3) + 60v → v = −2 m/s (2 m/s in the opposite direction).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key (sample): 1) p of 0.5 kg ball at 8 m/s = 4 kg·m/s. 2) 1,000 kg car at 20 m/s hits and sticks to 1,500 kg car at rest → 8 m/s. 3) impulse to stop a 0.15 kg ball at 30 m/s = 4.5 N·s. 4) airbags increase stopping time, reducing force. 5) 3 kg cart at 4 m/s and 1 kg cart at −2 m/s stick → v = (12 − 2)/4 = 2.5 m/s. 6) gun recoil explained by conservation of momentum.

weeks.prep: Raw eggs (several), toy car or small cart, straws, paper, tape, rubber bands; a ramp (board on books) and a wall/book as a barrier. Kitchen scale. Put down newspaper.
misconceptions: Making the device as stiff as possible. Crumple zones work by deforming to lengthen stopping time; rigid structures transfer force to the egg.
Changing several variables between tests. Change one design feature at a time so you know what caused the improvement.

days.guide: Together list criteria (egg survives a crash from a set ramp height) and constraints (e.g., 20 straws, 1 m tape, mass limit 100 g, egg must be visible).

questions.q: What is the difference between a criterion and a constraint?
questions.a: A criterion is what the design must achieve (egg doesn't crack); a constraint is a limit (materials, mass, time, cost).

days.guide: The student sketches three designs and scores them in a decision matrix (weighted criteria: protection, mass, buildability). Today's task from the plan: Sketch three designs and choose one using a decision matrix. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why use a decision matrix?
questions.a: It compares designs against the criteria objectively instead of choosing the favorite.

days.guide: Build and test from the set ramp height. Film the crash to estimate stopping time. Today's task from the plan: Build a prototype and test it in a ramp crash; record results. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Which physics principle should guide the design?
questions.a: Impulse: increase the stopping time (crumple zones, padding) to reduce the force on the egg, since F = Δp/Δt.

days.guide: Redesign one feature based on test data and retest. Estimate the impulse and average force. Today's task from the plan: Redesign based on test data and retest; calculate impulse reductions. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: If the redesign doubles the stopping time, how does the average force change?
questions.a: It halves (same Δp).

days.guide: The student presents the design (5 minutes) and takes the Unit 1 test. Today's task from the plan: Present the design and take the Unit 1 test. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Why do modern cars have crumple zones but rigid passenger cages?
questions.a: Crumple zones deform to increase stopping time and absorb energy, while the rigid cage prevents intrusion into the passenger space.

weeks.assessment_key: Design report rubric (4-point per row): problem definition with criteria/constraints; design selection with decision matrix; test data (at least two trials) and redesign based on evidence; explanation using impulse-momentum. Unit 1 test key (sample): kinematics (from rest a = 2 m/s² for 6 s → 12 m/s, 36 m), F = ma, free-body diagrams, third-law pairs, μ calculation, momentum conservation, impulse.

weeks.prep: Objects of different mass (ball, book, crumpled paper), stopwatch or phone video, measuring tape; flashlight, graph paper; PhET Gravity Force Lab.
misconceptions: Believing heavier objects fall faster. Without air resistance all objects fall with the same acceleration g; air resistance explains the paper.
Thinking there's no gravity in space (on the ISS). Gravity there is about 90% of surface gravity; astronauts float because they are in free fall.

days.guide: Drop objects from a measured height (e.g., 2.0 m), time several trials, and compute g = 2d/t². Today's task from the plan: Drop objects of different mass; measure g from timed drops. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: An object falls 2.0 m in 0.64 s. Estimate g.

days.guide: Shine a flashlight through a square hole in a card at the graph paper; double the distance and count squares lit. Today's task from the plan: Model inverse square law by shining a flashlight on graph paper at increasing distances. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: At twice the distance, how many times as many squares are lit, and what happens to brightness per square?
questions.a: 4 times the area, so each square gets 1/4 the light: intensity ∝ 1/r².

days.guide: Model F = Gm₁m₂/r² with scientific notation. Today's task from the plan: Calculate gravitational force between Earth and Moon and between two people. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Find the force between Earth (5.97 × 10²⁴ kg) and Moon (7.35 × 10²² kg) at 3.84 × 10⁸ m.
Force between two 70 kg people 1 m apart?
questions.a: ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻⁷ N, far too small to notice.

days.guide: In PhET, double one mass then double the distance; record the force each time. Today's task from the plan: Use PhET Gravity Force Lab to explore F vs. mass and distance. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: If the distance between two masses triples, how does the force change?
questions.a: It becomes 1/9 as large.

days.guide: Give the gravitation quiz. Today's task from the plan: Quiz on gravitation calculations. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: If both masses double and distance doubles, what happens to F?
questions.a: F × (2 × 2)/2² = F: unchanged.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key (sample): 1) g ≈ 9.8 m/s². 2) halving distance → 4× force. 3) doubling one mass → 2× force. 4) weight of 50 kg person = 490 N. 5) Earth–Sun force ≈ 3.5 × 10²² N (using M_sun 1.99 × 10³⁰ kg, r 1.5 × 10¹¹ m). 6) why astronauts float (free fall).

weeks.prep: String, two pushpins, cardboard; planet data table (semi-major axis in AU and period in years); PhET Gravity and Orbits.
misconceptions: Thinking seasons come from Earth's distance to the Sun. Earth's orbit is nearly circular (e ≈ 0.017); seasons are from axial tilt.
Thinking a satellite needs fuel to stay in orbit. It is continuously falling around Earth; its sideways speed keeps it from hitting the ground.

days.guide: Draw ellipses with pins at different spacings. e = c/a (focus distance ÷ semi-major axis). Today's task from the plan: Draw ellipses with string and pins; calculate eccentricity. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: An ellipse has a = 10 cm and foci 4 cm from the center. What is e?

days.guide: The student computes T² and a³ for each planet (AU, years) and graphs. Today's task from the plan: Analyze planet data to verify Kepler's third law (T² ∝ a³). Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Mars has a = 1.52 AU. Predict its period.
questions.a: T² = a³ = 3.51 → T ≈ 1.87 years.

days.guide: In PhET, increase the Sun's mass and observe Earth's orbit. Today's task from the plan: Use PhET Gravity and Orbits to change the Sun's mass and observe orbit changes. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: What happens to Earth's orbit if the Sun's mass doubles (at the same speed)?
questions.a: Stronger gravity pulls Earth into a smaller, faster, more elliptical orbit.

days.guide: Model v = √(GM/r) and T = 2πr/v for the ISS (about 400 km up). Today's task from the plan: Calculate orbital speed and period for the ISS and GPS satellites. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Find the ISS's orbital speed and period (r ≈ 6.77 × 10⁶ m, GM = 3.99 × 10¹⁴).
questions.a: v ≈ 7.7 km/s; T ≈ 92 minutes.

questions.q: Why do GPS satellites (about 20,200 km up) have longer periods?
questions.a: Larger r means weaker gravity and slower speed over a longer path; period ≈ 12 hours.

days.guide: The student writes an explanation of speed changes in an elliptical orbit. Today's task from the plan: Write an explanation of how orbital speed changes in an elliptical orbit. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Where is a planet fastest?
questions.a: At perihelion (closest to the Sun), as Kepler's second law requires equal areas in equal times.

weeks.assessment_key: Data analysis key: T²/a³ ≈ 1 for all planets in years and AU (Mercury 0.387 AU, 0.241 yr; Jupiter 5.20 AU, 11.86 yr). Rubric (4-point): table complete, graph of T² vs a³ linear through origin, slope ≈ 1, explanation of Kepler's second law with perihelion/aphelion speeds.

weeks.prep: Balloons, wool cloth, clear tape, aluminum foil, a glass jar, paper clip, cardboard lid. PhET Coulomb's Law. Dry days work best.
misconceptions: Thinking charging creates charge. Charging transfers electrons from one object to another; total charge is conserved.
Thinking only charged objects are attracted. A charged balloon attracts neutral paper bits by polarizing them (induced charge separation).

days.guide: Rub balloons on wool; test balloon-balloon (repel) and balloon-wall (attract). Make tape strips (top 'T' and bottom 'B') and test. Today's task from the plan: Charge balloons and tape strips; observe attraction and repulsion. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why do two balloons rubbed on wool repel each other?
questions.a: Both gain extra electrons (negative charge); like charges repel.

days.guide: In PhET, vary charge and distance; record force. Today's task from the plan: Use PhET Coulomb's Law to explore force vs. charge and distance. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: If the distance between two charges is halved, what happens to the force?
questions.a: It becomes 4 times larger (inverse square).

days.guide: Compare F_e and F_g for two protons using the formulas. Today's task from the plan: Compare gravitational and electrostatic forces between protons. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How many times stronger is the electric force than gravity between two protons?
questions.a: About 1.2 × 10³⁶ times (distance cancels since both follow 1/r²).

days.guide: Build the foil-leaf electroscope; test conduction (touch) and induction (bring near). Today's task from the plan: Build a foil-leaf electroscope in a jar and test charging by conduction and induction. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Why do the foil leaves spread apart when a charged balloon touches the top?
questions.a: Charge spreads to both leaves; like charges repel.

days.guide: Unit 2 test. Today's task from the plan: Unit 2 test on gravitation, orbits, and Coulomb's law. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Compare Newton's law of gravitation and Coulomb's law.
questions.a: Both are inverse-square laws; gravity is only attractive and acts between masses, while electric forces can attract or repel and act between charges.

weeks.assessment_key: Electroscope rubric: built correctly, tested both methods, explanation of electron movement. Unit 2 test key (sample): F_g calculations, Kepler's third law, orbital speed, inverse-square effects, Coulomb's law (two 1 μC charges 0.1 m apart: 0.90 N), conduction vs induction.

weeks.prep: Stairs (measure height of each step), stopwatch, bathroom scale. Remind the student to run safely.
misconceptions: Thinking carrying a box across a room at constant height does work against gravity. Work requires force in the direction of displacement.
Confusing power with energy. Power is the rate (energy per time).

days.guide: Model W = Fd cos θ. The student calculates work lifting and pushing. Today's task from the plan: Calculate work done lifting and pushing objects. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How much work to lift a 10 kg box 2.0 m?

days.guide: Model KE and PE for a coaster. Today's task from the plan: Calculate KE and PE for a roller coaster; relate to particle motion and fields. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: A 1,000 kg coaster moves at 20 m/s. Find its KE.
What is the PE of a 500 kg car at the top of a 30 m hill?

days.guide: Measure stair height, weigh the student, time running up. P = mgh/t. Today's task from the plan: Run up stairs timed; calculate personal power output in watts and horsepower. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: A 60 kg student climbs 3.0 m in 2.0 s. Power?

days.guide: Draw energy bar charts for skier, pendulum, spring. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: At the lowest point of a pendulum's swing, which energy is maximum?
questions.a: Kinetic energy.

days.guide: Energy quiz. Today's task from the plan: Quiz on energy calculations. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: A 2 kg ball is dropped from 5 m. What is its speed just before hitting the ground (ignore air resistance)?

weeks.assessment_key: Stair lab rubric: measurements with units, correct calculation, comparison to 746 W/hp, error sources. Quiz key (sample): work 50 N × 4 m = 200 J; KE of 0.5 kg at 6 m/s = 9 J; PE of 3 kg at 10 m = 294 J; power 1,200 J in 4 s = 300 W.

weeks.prep: PhET Energy Skate Park; foam pipe insulation (cut in half lengthwise) and marbles; spreadsheet; string and a mass for a pendulum; phone for slow-motion video.
misconceptions: Thinking energy disappears due to friction. It is transformed into thermal energy; total energy is conserved.
Using mass in v = √(2gh). Mass cancels.

days.guide: In PhET, observe energy bars with and without friction. Today's task from the plan: Use PhET Energy Skate Park to track KE, PE, and thermal energy. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Where does energy go when friction is turned on?
questions.a: Into thermal energy; total energy stays constant.

days.guide: Build the marble coaster; predict speed at the bottom of each hill from drop heights. Today's task from the plan: Build a foam pipe-insulation marble roller coaster and predict speeds at points. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: A marble drops 0.50 m. Predict its speed at the bottom (no friction).

days.guide: Build a spreadsheet: drop height → predicted speed. Today's task from the plan: Build a spreadsheet model predicting the speed of a pendulum from drop height. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Predict speed for a 0.20 m drop.
